items: Recognize that aggression stems from reactive brain responses rather than intentional ones—a child cannot access impulse control before acting.
Understand that the prefrontal cortex is only about 5% developed at this stage, not reaching full maturity until the mid-twenties.
Accept that asking "Why did you do that?" doesn't work because their brain literally cannot provide a reason before the behavior.
Remember that your toddler isn't giving you a hard time—they're having a hard time, and the aggression is neurological, not personal.
Replace "no hitting" with "Hands are gentle" or "We use gentle touches" so their brain holds the positive image instead.
Shift from "don't throw" to "Toys stay on the ground" to give your child a clear, positive behavior to follow.
Use "Feet stay on the floor" instead of "don't run" because positive commands give your toddler a specific target to meet.
Practice these positive scripts in the mirror tonight so the language feels natural when you need it in the moment.
Physically move away from aggressive behavior with a clear statement like "I have to protect my body" until your child can be safe.
Identify hunger, tiredness, overstimulation, or emotional overwhelm as underlying triggers and address them before frustration builds.
Manage your own nervous system during conflicts because toddlers need a calm adult to help them regulate, not escalate.
Connect with PCIT or a child behavior specialist if aggression feels unmanageable—they can provide structured support for your family.
